1.sense: The surah opens with a verb already glorifying before any subject is named: everything in the heavens and everything in the earth is doing it, without exception. The declaration precedes the surah's long account of a specific event, setting what follows inside a frame of Allah's power and wisdom. The same sentence closes the surah at its last verse.

notes.t: The verb is in the perfect tense, sabbaḥa rather than yusabbiḥu, so the glorifying is stated as a settled fact rather than an ongoing action described as it happens.
The same sentence, word for word, opens the surah immediately before this one.

links.why: the identical opening sentence, one surah earlier
the surah closes on the same pairing of names it opens on

2.sense: The verse names the event the surah is built around: the exile of Banu an-Nadir from Medina, called here the first gathering because a second and larger gathering of the People of the Book out of Arabia was still to come. Two expectations collapse in one sentence, the believers did not expect the exile, and the tribe did not expect their own fortresses to fail them. The houses come down by both sides' hands, theirs and the believers', and the verse ends by naming the reader directly, calling on whoever can see to look at what happened.

notes.t: Al-ḥashr, the gathering, is the surah's name and also names the Day of Judgment elsewhere in the Qur'an; using it here for a tribe's expulsion from Medina reads the event as a small preview of that larger gathering.
The same collapse, fortresses no defense, terror cast into hearts, is described again for Banu Qurayza, a different Medinan Jewish tribe, later in the same year.
The verse closes by naming its audience directly, ulī al-abṣār, possessors of sight, the only imperative addressed to the reader in the whole account.

links.why: the same word for their expulsion from their homes, used again of the emigrants who suffered it themselves

3.sense: The exile counts as mercy by comparison. Had Allah not already written banishment as their fate, a harsher punishment would have met them in this life, and the punishment of the Fire in the next one still stands regardless. The verse reframes what looked like a military outcome as something decreed beforehand.

notes.t: Al-jalāʾ, exile, is a civil term for leaving one's land, distinct from the words the Qur'an uses for war or killing; the verse insists this outcome was a decree, not simply the result of a siege.
The same pairing is used elsewhere: disgrace in this world matched with a great punishment in the next, there for those who bar people from Allah's mosques.

links.why: the same pairing, disgrace in this world alongside punishment in the next

4.sense: The verse names the cause behind what has just been described: they set themselves against Allah and His Messenger, and that opposition, not merely the fighting, is what brought the outcome. The clause then widens from this one tribe to a general rule that applies to anyone in the same position.

notes.t: Shāqqa is to put oneself on the opposite side, shiqq, of someone, a term for a standing rift rather than a single act of disobedience.
The same sentence, word for word, appears earlier in the Qur'an about a different confrontation, the disbelievers at Badr.

links.why: the identical sentence used earlier of the disbelievers at Badr
the same closing phrase, severe in punishment, returns three verses later

5.sense: The verse settles a question the siege had raised: cutting down productive palm trees was normally forbidden, so felling some of Banu an-Nadir's orchard while leaving the rest standing needed defending. Both choices, cutting and leaving, are placed under the same permission, so neither was a lapse. The disgrace named at the end belongs to the tribe, not to whoever felled the trees.

notes.t: Bukhari and Muslim record that the Prophet ﷺ ordered some palm trees of Banu an-Nadir burned and cut during the siege, which the besieged tribe protested as corruption; this verse answers that objection.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, Book of Maghāzī, from Ibn ʿUmar

notes.t: Līna is thought by some commentators to name a particular variety of date palm apart from the choicest kind, ʿajwa, and by others to cover palm trees in general; the exegetes differ on its exact scope.

links.why: the same siege this verse's detail belongs to, narrated two verses earlier

6.sense: The verse settles who the abandoned property of Banu an-Nadir belongs to. It came to the Prophet ﷺ without a battle, no cavalry charge, no camel drive, so the normal division of war spoils among the fighters does not apply, and the whole of it goes to him to distribute as fayʾ. The reason given is not tactics but Allah granting authority over whomever He wills.

notes.t: Fayʾ, from a root meaning to return, names property that comes to the Muslims without fighting, kept distinct throughout the surah from ghanīma, spoils taken in battle.
The Qur'an settles ownership of battle spoils the same way, as belonging to Allah and the Messenger to distribute, at the opening of Surah al-Anfal.

links.why: the distribution of this same fayʾ, spelled out by name in the next verse

7.sense: The rule widens from one tribe's abandoned land to fayʾ in general, taken from any town without a fight, and the distribution is fixed by name, Allah and the Messenger, relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, rather than left to the strongest claim. The stated purpose is that wealth not become dūla, a thing that only turns over among people already rich. The verse then generalizes further, past property, into a rule about obeying whatever the Messenger commands or forbids.

notes.t: Dūla shares its root with the modern word for a state, dawla; both come from a verb for turning something over from one hand to another.
The list of recipients here, Allah, the Messenger, near relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, matches word for word the list the Qur'an gives for the one-fifth share of battle spoils.
This is one of the few places the Qur'an states an economic purpose directly, that wealth not become something that only circulates among those already rich.

links.why: the identical recipient list, Allah, the Messenger, kin, orphans, the needy, the traveler, given there for a fifth of battle spoils
the parallel command to obey, paired there with obeying Allah and those in authority

8.sense: The share for Allah, the Messenger, and the needy named in the previous verse is now identified with a named group: the poor emigrants who left both home and property behind in Mecca. Their motive is given as bounty from Allah and His approval, alongside actively supporting Allah and His Messenger, and the verse closes by calling them, not just believers, but the truthful, people whose claim matches their conduct.

notes.t: Aṣ-ṣādiqūn, the truthful, is used here as a settled title rather than a description of one act, distinguishing a sincere claim to faith from the false one the surah goes on to describe in the hypocrites.
The same combination of emigration and active support for the cause with wealth and person is set out at length earlier, in the surah about the spoils of Badr.

links.why: the Medinan believers who housed them, described in the next verse with the same closing pattern, those, they, are

9.sense: This is the Ansar, the Medinans who had already made the city their home and held faith before the emigrants arrived. Their description moves through love of the newcomers, no resentment at what the newcomers were given, and preference for them over themselves even while in need. The verse ends on a general principle detached from the historical scene: whoever is spared his own soul's stinginess is among those who succeed.

notes.t: Bukhari and Muslim record that an Ansari host gave a hungry guest the only food in the house, feeding him in the dark so he would not see there was nothing left for the family, and that this verse was revealed about what he and his wife did.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah

notes.t: Tabawwaʾū is the verb for pitching a tent or claiming a dwelling place, used here for the Ansar's faith as much as their city, as though belief itself had become a home they had already moved into.

links.why: the emigrants this verse's love and preference are directed toward, named just before

10.sense: A third group is added to the emigrants and the Ansar: everyone who comes after them, defined only by a prayer rather than a deed. The prayer asks forgiveness for themselves and for those who believed earlier, and asks that no resentment settle in the heart toward believers generally. The verse gives later generations a place in the same list by words alone.

notes.t: Ghill is resentment that stays hidden below the surface rather than open hostility; asking that none of it be placed in the heart addresses a feeling rather than an action.

The same opening, rabbanā ighfir lanā, our Lord forgive us, is one of the Qur'an's most repeated prayers, said elsewhere by believers asking forgiveness for themselves together with those before them.

links.why: the brothers who preceded them in faith, described in the verse just before

11.sense: The scene shifts from Banu an-Nadir to the hypocrites in Medina who had promised them support in private. Their promise runs through three clauses, leaving together, obeying no outside authority, fighting alongside them, each stacked with an oath for emphasis. Allah's own testimony closes the verse and names the promise for what it is before events even test it.

notes.t: Each clause of the promise is built on a laʾin oath construction, the strongest form of conditional emphasis in Arabic, which the next verse takes apart clause by clause.
Swearing what is not meant is described elsewhere as the hypocrites' habitual behavior rather than a one-time lapse.

links.why: the promise made here is answered clause by clause in the next verse

12.sense: Each promise from the previous verse is answered in the same order and denied. They will not leave with them, will not aid them if attacked, and even the hypothetical case where they did aid them ends the same way: retreat, and no help left standing after that. The verse forecasts the outcome before Banu an-Nadir's exile plays it out.

notes.t: The three clauses mirror the three oaths of the previous verse in order and in grammar, so the denial reads as a direct answer rather than a separate statement.

links.why: the three promises this verse answers clause by clause

13.sense: The verse gives the reason behind the hypocrites' and the tribe's failure to back each other: the believers are feared more than Allah is. That fear, misplaced onto people rather than onto Allah, is traced to a failure of fiqh, of grasping how things actually stand.

notes.t: Yafqahūn comes from the same root as fiqh, understanding, later narrowed to the technical sense of jurisprudence; here it names the plain failure to grasp where real power lies.

links.why: the same closing formula, that is because they are a people who, repeats one verse later with a different failing named

14.sense: The picture continues past the failed alliance to the enemy's actual military posture: they will not meet the believers in open combat except behind walls, and their fierceness is reserved for fighting each other. Apparent unity hides real division, a gap the verse locates in the heart rather than on the surface. The closing formula changes the failing named from not understanding to not reasoning.

notes.t: Yafqahūn in the previous verse and yaʿqilūn here, understanding and reasoning, are near-synonyms in the Qur'an's vocabulary, so setting them side by side across two verses reads as one failure described twice rather than two different faults.
Hidden hostility greater than what shows on the surface is a warning given earlier about outsiders taken as close allies.

links.why: the same closing formula, with the failing changed from not understanding to not reasoning

15.sense: The comparison points to a recent precedent rather than an ancient one. Most commentators read this as Banu Qaynuqaʿ, another Jewish tribe of Medina expelled shortly before Banu an-Nadir under similar terms, so the tribe now facing exile had already watched the consequence play out once nearby. The painful punishment named at the end is still to come, separate from what they already tasted.

notes.t: Commentators differ on which recent precedent is meant: most read it as Banu Qaynuqaʿ, expelled from Medina not long before this surah's events, though some read it as the defeat of the Meccan disbelievers at Badr.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record both readings

notes.t: Wabāl is the bad outcome that a choice brings back on the one who made it, used elsewhere in the Qur'an for the consequence of a people's own conduct rather than an outside punishment.

links.why: the exile this verse's precedent is compared against

16.sense: A second comparison follows the first, this one about betrayal rather than precedent. Satan urges disbelief and then disowns the very person who took his word, citing fear of Allah as his excuse. The image fits the hypocrites' promise in verse 11 exactly: encouragement given freely, support withdrawn the moment it would cost something.

notes.t: The scene has no named setting or time; the exegetes take it as an image of how temptation generally works rather than one historical incident.
Satan disowning those who followed him is described again, at greater length, as a speech he gives on the Day of Judgment.

links.why: the fuller version of the same disowning, given as a speech on the Day of Judgment
the hypocrites' promise this comparison mirrors, encouragement offered and then withdrawn

words.g: the end of the two of them

17.sense: The two comparisons close together: Satan and the one he misled share one outcome, the Fire, permanently. The verse steps back from the image to name what it stands for, this is the standard reward for wrongdoing, not a fate specific to Satan and his one victim.

notes.t: ʿĀqibatahumā, the outcome of the two of them, uses the dual form, tying Satan and the misled person to one shared ending rather than two separate ones.

18.sense: The verse turns from the account of Banu an-Nadir to a direct address, the first in the surah aimed at the believers themselves. Fear of Allah frames both ends of the sentence, and between the two commands sits a single instruction: look at what has already been sent ahead for tomorrow, as though the record were something a person could go back and check now.

notes.t: Ghad, tomorrow, is used here for the Day of Judgment, the near word standing in for the far event to make the looking feel immediate rather than distant.
The same image, a soul confronted with what it sent ahead, appears again describing the moment the sky splits.

links.why: the same reckoning image, a soul facing what it sent ahead, set at the moment the sky splits

19.sense: The warning turns the same verb back on itself: forgetting Allah is answered with Allah making the forgetter forget his own self. The consequence is not punishment added from outside but a natural result of the original neglect, and it lands on the same title used for Banu an-Nadir earlier in the surah, the defiantly disobedient.

notes.t: The wordplay, nasū ... fa-ansāhum, forgot ... so He made them forget, makes the punishment mirror the offense in the sentence's own grammar.

links.why: the same closing title, al-fāsiqūn, used earlier of Banu an-Nadir

20.sense: The verse states a plain inequality between the two outcomes and then repeats the name of the winning side rather than simply naming both. Only the companions of Paradise get the second clause, called the successful, so the sentence ends weighted entirely toward one side.

notes.t: The repetition of aṣḥāb al-jannati rather than a pronoun keeps both the phrase and the outcome in view twice in one short verse.

21.sense: A hypothetical measures what the Qur'an is against something solid: a mountain receiving it would not stand unmoved but would crack apart in awe. The comparison points at the human audience that does receive the Qur'an without that visible reaction, and the verse names its own method in passing, these are amthāl, examples, given so that people will think them through.

notes.t: Khāshiʿan and mutaṣaddiʿan describe a living posture and a physical break together, giving the mountain both an emotional state and a fracture in the same two words.
Mountains are described elsewhere declining a trust the heavens and earth also refused, out of the same apprehension pictured here.

links.why: mountains again measured against something they cannot bear, there the Trust rather than the Qur'an

22.sense: The surah shifts into its closing sequence of divine names, opening each of its last three verses with huwa Allāh. This one moves from the single claim of exclusive godhood into knowledge that covers what is hidden and what is present without distinction, then to the pair of names built on mercy.

notes.t: Al-ghayb and ash-shahāda, the unseen and the witnessed, is a standing pair in the Qur'an's vocabulary for the whole of reality, not two separate categories of things known.
The same pairing, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, names Allah again earlier in the Qur'an.

links.why: the same opening formula, He is Allah, continues into the next verse's longer list of names

23.sense: Nine names run in sequence with no conjunction between them, an unbroken list rather than the paired names used elsewhere in the surah. The verse then turns from naming to a direct declaration, exalting Allah above whatever is set beside Him, which reads as the point the whole list has been building toward.

notes.t: The nine names run without any wa, and, joining them, a construction the Qur'an uses to give a listed description one continuous weight rather than a set of separate items.
The closing formula, exalted is He above what they associate with Him, recurs across the Qur'an as a fixed response to claims of partners with Allah.

links.why: the list of names continues, unbroken, into the surah's final verse

24.sense: Three names of making run together, bringing into being, shaping matter without a prior model, giving form, before the verse states outright that the best names all belong to Allah. The closing line returns to the opening sentence of the surah nearly word for word, so the whole chapter ends where it began, everything in the heavens and the earth glorifying Him.

notes.t: Khāliq, bāriʾ and muṣawwir move from the general act of creating, to shaping something out of matter, to giving it its particular form, three stages of the same act named separately.
The best names are named as a set again, with the instruction to call on Allah by them.

links.why: the closing sentence returns almost word for word to the surah's opening line
